correctness.rationale: The 2009 full text explicitly identifies the complete facet system for N>=3 and 1<k<N, so the full proof uses no speculative facet assumption. Orthogonal projection of coordinate and row/column normals onto the fixed-total tangent space gives squared norms 1-1/N² and N-1. Summing facet-clearance constraints gives two universal sharp upper bounds. Their exact equality cases force the uniform unique incenter below the threshold and exactly sJ+lambda B_N above it. The Birkhoff dimension and vertex counts are standard and the tangency statement follows from the same inequalities. A uniform convex barycenter of all k-assignment vertices proves the unique outer sphere in all dimensions. Independent LP and exhaustive small-vertex computations corroborate but do not replace the symbolic proof.

originality.rationale: The exact k-assignment H-representation and facet list were inspected in Gill--Linusson (2009), and the bipartite k-matching counterpart in Torres (2023), both as full text. The former derives dimension, face poset and graph diameter; the latter establishes normality, with no Euclidean-radius or incenter-locus statement. Indexed mathematical database and targeted literature searches under k-assignment, partial permutation, partial Birkhoff, doubly substochastic fixed-sum, Chebyshev-center, and inradius aliases returned no dominating statement. The closest compared matching and transportation metric invariants concern different polytopes or different affine metrics.
residual_risks: Classical assignment-polytope or fixed-total substochastic-matrix literature could encode an equivalent inradius calculation without the terms in the targeted searches.
The Frobenius facet-normal calculation is short once the H-representation and its facet table are known, allowing independent rediscovery.
Absence of an indexed match is evidence of an incomplete search, not a proof of global novelty.

value.rationale: The k-assignment polytope is a canonical fixed-cardinality matching and network-flow polytope, extensively studied for its facets, graph diameter, face lattice and normality. Its Euclidean robustness to entry and row/column capacity perturbations is naturally measured by the largest intrinsic ball. The theorem identifies a structural, not merely numerical, phase transition: low ranks have a unique center forced by every entry constraint, but high ranks admit an entire (N−1)^2-dimensional incenter polytope exactly homothetic to the Birkhoff polytope, including its vertices and coordinate-tangency strata. The outer ball remaining uniquely centered shows an informative asymmetry between the two Euclidean extremal-center problems.
